title: The Days of Creation and the Age of the Earth
lead: How long were the six days of Genesis 1, and how old is the world? Jews and Christians have answered in many ways, long before modern science and since. This page sets out each main view in its strongest form.

sections.b:
Ordinary days, a young earth. The days are 24-hour days, and the genealogies give an age of thousands of years (Basil, Luther, Calvin, Ussher; young-earth creationists today, such as Answers in Genesis and the Institute for Creation Research). Exodus 20:11 grounds the Sabbath in the week of creation; death came through sin (Romans 5:12). Most of the fossil record is attributed to the flood.

Long days (day-age). Each day is an age (Hugh Ross; Reasons to Believe). Yom can mean a period (Genesis 2:4), and the seventh day has no evening.

A gap before the days. A first creation, ruined, then six days of re-creation (Thomas Chalmers; the Scofield Bible). Few hold it now.

God's work-days (analogical). Real days of God's work, told by analogy to a human week (C. John Collins).

A literary framework. Days 1–3 form realms and days 4–6 fill them; the week arranges creation by topic (Augustine in part; Arie Noordtzij; Meredith Kline; Henri Blocher).

A temple inauguration. Seven days in which God gives the cosmos its functions as his temple and takes his rest (John Walton).

Ancient cosmology. Most critical scholars hold that the writer meant ordinary days within an ancient picture of the world, and that the text teaches theology, not science.

The scientific consensus dates the universe to about 13.8 billion years and the earth to about 4.5 billion years. Young-earth creationists dissent; the other views above accept that dating.
sections.refs: Genesis 1:1–2:3; Exodus 20:11; Exodus 31:17; Psalm 90:4; 2 Peter 3:8; Hebrews 4:3–10; Romans 5:12

sections.b: Jewish tradition has never had one doctrine of the days. Many rabbis and medieval commentators read them as ordinary days, and the Jewish calendar counts years from creation (3761 BC). But Genesis Rabbah records that God "was building worlds and destroying them" before this one (Genesis Rabbah 3:7; 9:2). Maimonides warned that not everything in the account of creation is to be taken in its plain sense (Guide of the Perplexed 2.29–30). Nachmanides (Ramban) read the six days also as a sign of six thousand years of history (on 2:3). In modern times Rav Abraham Isaac Kook wrote that an ancient universe and even evolution need not trouble faith; Aryeh Kaplan cited the medieval kabbalist Isaac of Acre for a universe billions of years old; and the physicist Gerald Schroeder has argued that six days and fifteen billion years can both be true from different frames of reference.

common: The church always taught that the days were 24 hours until Darwin.
The framework view denies that Genesis is true.
uncommon: Augustine thought God made everything in a single moment and that the days describe angels' knowledge of creation.
Some early Jewish and Christian writers (the Epistle of Barnabas 15; Irenaeus) read the six days as a prophecy of six thousand years of history, a "world-week," not as thousand-year creation days.
Medieval and modern Jewish thinkers, from Genesis Rabbah to Maimonides and Aryeh Kaplan, offered non-literal or old-universe readings long before the creation-evolution debate.
